content_voiceover: This slide classifies sideroblastic anemias, defined by pathologic iron deposits in erythroblast mitochondria, into hereditary and acquired forms. The classic hereditary cause is X-linked sideroblastic anemia, XLSA, from ALAS2 mutations, the same rate-limiting heme synthesis enzyme from the last slide, and the single most testable hereditary cause. Other hereditary causes include SLC25A38 and glutaredoxin 5 deficiency. Recognize these syndromic names, XLSA with ataxia from ABCB7 mutations disrupting iron-sulfur cluster maturation, MLASA, myopathy, lactic acidosis, sideroblastic anemia, SIFD, sideroblastic anemia with B-cell immunodeficiency, and Pearson syndrome, a mitochondrial cytopathy from large mitochondrial DNA deletions. On the acquired side, the major clonal cause is MDS with ring sideroblasts. But the high-yield exam favorite is reversible sideroblastic anemia, caused by alcoholism, lead poisoning, drugs like isoniazid, chloramphenicol, linezolid, and cyclosporine, copper deficiency, or hypothermia. These matter clinically because removing the cause, stopping the drug, adding pyridoxine for isoniazid, correcting copper, reverses the anemia.
keypoints: XLSA (ALAS2 mutation) = most common hereditary SA
ABCB7 -> XLSA/ataxia; mtDNA deletion -> Pearson syndrome
Reversible: alcohol, lead, isoniazid/chloramphenicol/linezolid, copper deficiency, hypothermia
keypoint_voiceover: Know XLSA from ALAS2 mutation as the classic hereditary sideroblastic anemia, and MDS with ring sideroblasts as the major acquired clonal cause. For exams, focus on reversible causes, alcohol, lead poisoning, drugs including isoniazid, chloramphenicol, linezolid, and cyclosporine, copper deficiency, and hypothermia. Isoniazid causes sideroblastic anemia through B6 antagonism, so it's treated with pyridoxine supplementation.
